title: Curiosity Beyond the Textbook
currentEventHeadline: Scientists keep finding surprises in places we thought we knew.
eventSummary: From new species discovered in well-studied forests to fresh insights from old experiments, ordinary scientists keep revising what we thought we knew. The pattern: curiosity + careful observation + willingness to revisit assumptions.
connectionToLesson: Today's lesson is one more chance to ask: what's the assumption I haven't questioned yet?
studentTask: In pairs, name one 'common knowledge' fact from this lesson. Then list ONE reason it might still be incomplete, and ONE way you could check.
discussionQuestions: What's the difference between 'something we don't know' and 'something we got wrong'?
Whose curiosity counted in this lesson — and whose was ignored?
If today's lesson turned out to be partly mistaken, how would we find out?
extensionActivity: Write a 3-sentence note to a scientist (alive or historical) who would have loved this lesson.
teacherNotes: Evergreen prompt. Source: Curriculate evergreen library.

title: Then & Now
currentEventHeadline: Decisions in the past still shape our headlines this week.
eventSummary: Every modern news story has roots — sometimes decades, sometimes centuries deep. Historians call this 'path dependency': the choices people made before us narrow the choices we have now.
connectionToLesson: Whatever you studied today probably echoes in a current debate. Your job is to find the echo.
studentTask: In pairs, name ONE event or person from today's lesson. Then describe how one of their choices STILL shapes a real debate today — give an example.
discussionQuestions: Whose choices in today's lesson had consequences far beyond what they intended?
Are we bound by past decisions, or can we always start over? What's the evidence?
If today's lesson had gone differently, what current debate might not exist?
extensionActivity: Find one headline from this week. Trace it back at least 100 years.
teacherNotes: Evergreen prompt for history/social studies. Source: Curriculate evergreen library.

title: Where Math Hides
currentEventHeadline: Math is doing invisible work behind every modern technology.
eventSummary: GPS, search engines, vaccines, even the playlist on your phone — they all rest on math most people never see. The breakthroughs that look 'tech' are usually math first.
connectionToLesson: Today's concepts are part of that invisible foundation. The question isn't 'when will I use this' — it's 'where is this ALREADY working without me noticing?'
studentTask: List ONE place today's math concept might be working invisibly RIGHT NOW (in this room, this building, your pocket).
discussionQuestions: What's something you used today that wouldn't exist without math you don't fully understand?
Is invisible math a kind of trust? What are we trusting?
Are there parts of life math doesn't (or shouldn't) touch?
extensionActivity: Pick one app on your phone. Hypothesize what math the developers must understand.
teacherNotes: Evergreen prompt for math. Source: Curriculate evergreen library.

title: Why This Story Lasted
currentEventHeadline: The stories that survive carry something the moment couldn't kill.
eventSummary: Most stories disappear. The ones that last across decades or centuries usually share something — a question that stays urgent, a character who stays surprising, language that still lands. Researchers call these 'sticky narratives'.
connectionToLesson: Today's reading lasted long enough for you to study it. Why? What did it carry that other stories from its time didn't?
studentTask: Pick ONE moment from today's reading. Argue (in 2-3 sentences) why a reader 50 years from now might still care about that moment.
discussionQuestions: What makes a story 'survive'? Quality, luck, who's in power, or something else?
Whose stories are most likely to disappear? Why?
If you could only save ONE story from today's lesson for the future, which? Why?
extensionActivity: Rewrite the opening sentence of today's reading as if it were a headline today. What changes? What doesn't?
teacherNotes: Evergreen prompt for ELA. Source: Curriculate evergreen library.

title: Old Words, Today's Streets
currentEventHeadline: Ancient wisdom keeps showing up in modern moral debates.
eventSummary: When journalists, judges, and ordinary people argue about what's right today, they often borrow language from texts that are thousands of years old. Sometimes faithfully — sometimes by accident.
connectionToLesson: Today's lesson is one such piece of borrowed language. Where is it showing up in this week's headlines?
studentTask: In pairs, name ONE current event you've heard about this week. Connect it (specifically) to today's lesson — even if the headline doesn't mention it.
discussionQuestions: When today's lesson talks about justice / mercy / wisdom, is it saying the same thing modern news does?
Where does today's lesson surprise you compared to how the same idea gets used now?
If everyone read today's text, would this week's news be different? Why or why not?
extensionActivity: Find one phrase from today's lesson that you've heard people use OUTSIDE of class. What did they mean by it?
teacherNotes: Evergreen prompt for religion/Bible/ministry classes. Source: Curriculate evergreen library.

title: The Code Underneath
currentEventHeadline: Every screen you tap is the tip of an iceberg of code someone wrote.
eventSummary: What looks like 'just an app' is usually tens of millions of lines of code, built by thousands of people over decades. Each line is a decision someone made — and those decisions are now invisible defaults shaping your life.
connectionToLesson: Today's concept is one of those underlying decisions. Most people will never see it. You will.
studentTask: Pick ONE feature on a phone or laptop. Name a decision the engineers must have made — and what could go wrong if they got it wrong.
discussionQuestions: What's the difference between 'how something works' and 'how it was designed to work'?
Who's accountable when the invisible default is wrong?
Could you re-design today's concept differently? What would change?
extensionActivity: Read one app's privacy policy or terms of service. Highlight one decision the engineers made for you.
teacherNotes: Evergreen prompt for CS/tech. Source: Curriculate evergreen library.

title: Why Art Lasts
currentEventHeadline: Art that lasts usually said something that mattered when nobody else would say it.
eventSummary: The artists, musicians, and writers we still talk about often pushed something into the open before it was safe — a question, an emotion, a perspective. Some were celebrated then; some weren't. The work outlived the moment either way.
connectionToLesson: Today's work is one of those that lasted. Why?
studentTask: Pick ONE moment from today's lesson. Argue (in 2 sentences) what made it brave or unusual when it was made.
discussionQuestions: What art do you think people will still care about in 100 years? Why?
Is comfortable art ever great art? When?
Who decides what art lasts? Should we trust them?
extensionActivity: Find one piece of art (music / image / writing) made THIS year that takes a risk. What is the risk?
teacherNotes: Evergreen prompt for arts. Source: Curriculate evergreen library.

title: What We Know That We Didn't
currentEventHeadline: Health advice we follow today would have sounded radical 30 years ago.
eventSummary: Sleep matters more than we thought. Sitting all day is worse than we thought. Exercise helps the brain, not just the body. These shifts didn't happen because new bodies appeared — they happened because researchers asked sharper questions.
connectionToLesson: Today's lesson is one of those sharper questions. What does it ask you to update?
studentTask: Name ONE thing in today's lesson that contradicts what you (or someone you know) used to believe. What evidence would change your mind further?
discussionQuestions: What health 'common sense' from 30 years ago is now considered wrong?
Why do health beliefs change so slowly even when the evidence shifts?
Who do you trust for health information? Should you?
extensionActivity: Find one piece of health advice your parents grew up with. Look up whether researchers still agree.
teacherNotes: Evergreen prompt for health/PE. Source: Curriculate evergreen library.

title: Why Markets Move
currentEventHeadline: Markets react to news, but they really move on what people THINK others will think.
eventSummary: Stock prices, currency values, even housing prices — they don't just respond to facts. They respond to predictions about predictions. Economist John Maynard Keynes called this a 'beauty contest': don't pick what you think is best, pick what you think others will pick.
connectionToLesson: Today's concept is one piece of how that game gets played.
studentTask: Name ONE recent news event you've heard about. Describe how it might be moving prices — even before anything 'actually' changes.
discussionQuestions: If markets move on belief, are they a measure of reality or of mood?
When does the beauty-contest dynamic help us? When does it hurt us?
Should anyone be steering this? Who would you trust to?
extensionActivity: Pick one product you buy. Hypothesize what would have to happen in the news for its price to double next month.
teacherNotes: Evergreen prompt for business/economics. Source: Curriculate evergreen library.

title: What's New This Week?
currentEventHeadline: Cool things keep being discovered, even by people just like you.
eventSummary: Real scientists, real explorers, and real ordinary people keep finding new things every single week. Most discoveries don't make the front page — but they're real.
connectionToLesson: Today you learned something new. So did somebody else, somewhere — maybe a kid your age.
studentTask: Tell a partner ONE thing you learned today. Then ask them what THEY think someone else might be learning right now.
discussionQuestions: What's the most interesting thing you learned this week — in or out of school?
Where do new discoveries come from?
What would you like to discover one day?
extensionActivity: Draw a picture of something you'd like someone to discover.
teacherNotes: Evergreen prompt for younger grades. Source: Curriculate evergreen library.
